title: Two ways to build a verb
goal: Master the most distinctive feature of Hungarian, one with no counterpart in any language you have likely studied: two sets of verb endings, chosen by whether the object is definite or not.
bekal: build the definite form for every person
use the special *-lak / -lek* form for "I … you"

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Az étteremben
dialogs.intro: A small restaurant on Kazinczy utca. Anna comes here often; Budi has never been.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'll have a soup. And you?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Én a gulyást kérem. Azt mindig szeretem.
lines.id: I'll have the goulash. I always love it.
lines.literal: I the goulash-obj I-ask-it. that-obj always I-love-it.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Igen, jól ismerem. Gyakran eszem itt.
lines.id: Yes, I know it well. I often eat here.
lines.literal: yes, well I-know-it. often I-eat here.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Érted az étlapot? Én nem értek semmit.
lines.id: Do you understand the menu? I don't understand anything.
lines.literal: you-understand-it the menu-obj? I not I-understand nothing-obj.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: Sure. I'll read it out for you.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you! And what are you drinking?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Egy pohár bort kérek. Te is kérsz bort?
lines.id: I'll have a glass of wine. Do you want wine too?
lines.literal: a glass wine-obj I-ask. you too you-ask wine-obj?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nem, én vizet kérek. Nem iszom alkoholt.
lines.id: No, I'll have water. I don't drink alcohol.
lines.literal: no, I water-obj I-ask. not I-drink alcohol-obj.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: All right. Then I'll call the waiter.

notes: **Reread the dialogue and watch one thing only: when Anna says *kérek* and when she says *kérem*.** *Egy levest kérek* — no particular soup yet, so the indefinite form. *A gulyást kérem* — the goulash on the menu, a definite one, so the definite form. The difference is not about politeness or number; it is about whether the object has a clear identity.

**English marks the same thing another way.** Compare "I'll have **a** soup" and "I'll have **the** soup". In English the article on the **noun** does the work; Hungarian marks it on the **verb** as well.

**The trigger for the definite form is always in the object.** The article *a/az*, the demonstratives *ezt/azt*, a proper name, a possessive ending, or the pronouns *őt/őket* — if any of these appears, the verb must take the definite form. There are no exceptions to memorize at A1.

**Nem értek semmit** uses the indefinite form even though *nem* is there. The trigger is not the negation but *semmit* (nothing), the most indefinite object there is. Compare *Nem értem* ("I don't understand" — the thing just said, so definite).

**Elolvasom neked** uses the definite form without naming the object. The object is hidden: "I'll read **it** for you". When a definite object is obvious from the situation, Hungarian drops it but keeps the definite form — and that is exactly the point. The verb form itself carries the information.

grammars.title: The definite form — the second set of endings
body: Compare with the table in unit 10. Same persons, same vowel groups; the whole tail is different.
after: **Back-vowel verbs use j, front-vowel verbs use i.** Compare *tanulja* with *kéri*, *tanulják* with *kérik*. The only row with *j* in both groups is the *mi* row: *tanuljuk*, *kérjük*.

**J merges after s, sz, z, dz.** *olvas* + *ja* → *olvas**sa***; *olvas* + *juk* → *olvas**suk***; *néz* + *jük* → *néz**zük***; *főz* + *jük* → *főz**zük***. The reason is the same as in unit 10: Hungarian avoids piling up hissing sounds.

grammars.title: When to use which
body: One table worth bookmarking — you will come back to it many times in the next few weeks.

head: If the object…
Set
Example
rows: there is no object at all

after: **The fastest check:** put your sentence into English and see whether the noun naturally takes "the", "this", "my" or a name. "I'll have the soup" → definite. "I'll have a soup" / "I'll have soup" → indefinite. This check is right nine times out of ten.

**Note the ninth row.** *Engem*, *téged*, *minket*, *titeket* are objects whose person is perfectly clear, yet they take the **indefinite** set. This is the one part you truly have to memorize, because common sense misleads you here.

grammars.title: Szeretlek — the special "I … you" form
body: There is a third form that stands on its own, used only when **I** do something to **you**.
after: The ending is *-lak / -lek*, and it replaces every other ending. Note that *téged* (you, as object) can be added for emphasis but is not required: *Téged várlak* = "it's you I'm waiting for".

*Kérlek* is one of the most useful words in everyday Hungarian. It means "please" when you ask a friend for something, while the polite form is *kérem*. These two words cover almost every request you will make.

sections.title: Eight pairs that show the difference

blocks.text: Read each row aloud, both sentences in a row. Your ear picks up this pattern much faster than your eye.

blocks.title: Three questions, in order
items: **Is there an object?** If not, you're done — use the indefinite form.
**Does the object have *a/az*, a demonstrative, a proper name, or a possessive ending?** If so, use the definite form.
**Is the object *engem, téged, minket, titeket*?** If so, use the indefinite form — even though the person is clear.

blocks.text: Those three questions settle almost every A1 sentence. What's left — subordinate clauses, odd indefinite pronouns, nested structures — comes naturally at A2, and until then it will never get in the way of your conversations.

One last thing worth knowing now so it doesn't confuse you later: this double set also applies in the **past tense** (unit 18) and in the imperative. So the effort you put into this unit pays off three times, not once.
